name: Sir Robert W Philip Plaque
description: This blue plaque near The Mound commemorates Dr Robert William Philip, who in 1887 founded the Victoria Dispensary for Consumption and Diseases of the Chest nearby - the world's first clinic dedicated specifically to fighting tuberculosis. Rather than simply treating patients as they arrived, Philip pioneered what became known as the Edinburgh Scheme: tracing a disease back through a patient's household and social circumstances, examining infected families, and working to contain outbreaks at their source, treating tuberculosis as a public health problem to be managed at population scale rather than case by case.
interesting_fact: The plaque itself was erected in 1957, the centenary of Philip's birth, by the National Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis, and quotes his own confident prediction that mankind would eventually master the disease. His dispensary model - combining outpatient treatment, home visits, and a linked sanatorium and after-care colony - was so influential it was copied around the world and became the template for modern tuberculosis-control programmes, decades before antibiotics existed to actually cure the disease he spent his career trying to contain.

name: Old Assembly Close
description: Old Assembly Close was originally called Little's Close, after the brothers Clement and William Little, before Edinburgh's dancing assembly - which began in 1723 - gave it its present name. The great hall here hosted the city's high society balls until the assembly moved to New Assembly Close in 1736, and the original hall was later destroyed in the Great Fire of 1824, which started in an engraver's workshop in this very close.
interesting_fact: The 1824 fire began when a pot of overheated linseed oil in James Kirkwood's engraving workshop set a stack of paper alight - within hours the flames had spread along the High Street rooftops, fanned by a southwesterly wind.

name: Borthwick's Close
description: Borthwick's Close is one of the many narrow medieval closes running off the High Street near St Giles' Cathedral and Parliament Square, most named after a resident merchant, tradesman, or landowner whose identity has often been lost to time. Like its neighbours, it was built to squeeze maximum tenement housing into a tight sliver of Old Town street frontage.
interesting_fact: Closes like this one were sealed at night by a locked gate at the street end - hence the name 'close' - a security measure for the crowded, largely self-contained communities living up the shared stairs above.

name: Statue of James Braidwood
description: This bronze statue in Parliament Square honours James Braidwood (1800-1861), who in 1824 became the first Master of Engines of Edinburgh's fire brigade - the world's first municipal fire service. Braidwood introduced protective helmets and uniforms and pioneered the then-radical idea of training firefighters to enter burning buildings rather than simply spraying water from outside.
interesting_fact: Braidwood later became head of the London Fire Engine Establishment and died fighting a warehouse fire on Tooley Street in 1861, aged 61, when a collapsing wall killed him - the statue was unveiled in 2008, funded by a former Lothian & Borders Firemaster.

name: The Supreme Courts
description: Behind Parliament Square's facade lies Parliament House, built on the orders of Charles I and completed in 1639 as the seat of the pre-Union Scottish Parliament - the world's first purpose-built parliament building. Since the Union of 1707 it has housed Scotland's supreme courts, the Court of Session and High Court of Justiciary, spread across more than 700 rooms behind the historic frontage.
interesting_fact: Parliament Hall, the oldest part of the complex, has a magnificent hammer-beam oak ceiling and still serves lawyers today as a 'salle des pas perdus' - a hall for pacing and informal conference between court appearances, a tradition unbroken for nearly 200 years.

name: Charles II Statue
description: This lead equestrian statue of Charles II, erected in 1685 - the year of his death - is believed to be the oldest statue in Edinburgh and possibly the oldest lead equestrian statue in Britain. It depicts the king in Roman military dress, carrying a baton as a symbol of imperial authority, on a pedestal carved from Craigleith stone by Robert Mylne, the King's Master Mason.
interesting_fact: Charles II's own path to the throne ran through Edinburgh: after his father's execution in 1649, the Scottish Parliament proclaimed him king, but Cromwell crushed his forces at the Battle of Worcester in 1651, forcing him into exile until the monarchy's restoration in 1660.

name: Roxburgh's Close
description: Roxburgh's Close is thought to take its name from John Roxburgh, a chef recorded living here in 1635. Like many Old Town closes it fell out of everyday use for long stretches as surrounding buildings changed hands and function, before being reopened as part of later redevelopment of the Royal Mile's historic street pattern.
interesting_fact: The closes running off the Royal Mile were never simple back alleys - each was effectively its own tiny neighbourhood, with tenement stairs holding dozens of households stacked above shops and workshops at street level.

description: Bank of Scotland's headquarters has crowned the top of the Mound since 1806, when architects Robert Reid and Richard Crichton - both former pupils of Robert Adam - completed a domed Georgian villa on land the bank bought from the city in 1800. interesting_fact: Founded in 1695, Bank of Scotland is one of the oldest banks in the world still trading under its original name, and its Mound headquarters remains the registered Scottish office of Lloyds Banking Group today.

name: Milne's Court
description: Milne's Court, built in 1692 by Robert Milne, master mason to the king, was the first open courtyard of its kind in Edinburgh - a deliberate break from the cramped, enclosed closes surrounding it. The original west range was demolished in 1883, but the University of Edinburgh restored the north and south blocks and rebuilt the east range between 1966 and 1970, turning the court into student accommodation.
interesting_fact: Milne's Court set the template that later, grander courtyards like James' Court and Riddle's Court would follow - proof that even in the crowded 17th-century Old Town, there was appetite for a bit more light and air.
